# Method for Configuring Memory Pools with Referenced Entries

## Overview

The disclosed method establishes a two-tier memory architecture wherein two distinct pools of memory are configured to work in concert: a first pool that stores primary data entries, and a second pool that provides an efficient referencing mechanism to access those entries. This architecture enables flexible and compact addressing even when the underlying data organization varies in granularity across different memory locations.

## Configuration of the First Memory Pool

The method begins by configuring a first pool of memories to implement a first set of entries. This first pool may comprise one or more individual memory devices or memory banks, collectively referred to as "first-pool memories." Each entry within the first set is physically located at a specific, identifiable location within at least one of these first-pool memories. This arrangement allows the first pool to serve as the underlying storage layer, housing the actual data content that will later be accessed through the reference mechanism established in the second pool.

## Configuration of the Second Memory Pool

Building upon the first pool, the method further configures a second pool of memories to implement a second set of entries. Critically, each entry in this second set does not store data directly; rather, it serves as a reference or pointer to a corresponding entry in the first set. This indirection layer allows the second pool to function as an indexing or lookup structure, enabling efficient navigation to the appropriate data stored in the first pool.

## Structure of Second-Set Entries

Each entry in the second set is structured to contain multiple distinct bit fields, each serving a specific addressing function:

### First Set of Bits: Memory Page Identification

The first set of bits within each second-set entry indicates a memory page that corresponds to one or more of the first-pool memories. This field effectively identifies which memory page—and by extension, which specific first-pool memory or memories—contains the target data referenced by this entry. This page-level identification serves as the coarsest level of addressing granularity within the reference structure.

### Second Set of Bits: Location Specification

The second set of bits specifies a particular location within each of the one or more memories identified by the first set of bits. This field narrows the addressing scope from the page level down to a specific location within that page, indicating precisely where the data for the referenced first-set entry can be retrieved. Together, the first and second sets of bits provide sufficient information to locate the retrieved data at a coarse-to-medium granularity.

### Third Set of Bits: Sub-Location Specification

The third set of bits provides an additional, finer level of addressing precision by specifying a sub-location within the data retrieved based on the second set of bits. This field allows the reference entry to point not merely to a general location, but to a specific sub-component or segment within the data retrieved from that location—enabling more granular access to structured or partitioned data.

## Fixed-Width Design of the Sub-Location Field

A key architectural feature of this method is that the number of bits allocated to the third set of bits remains fixed and consistent across all entries in the second set. This uniformity is maintained even though the actual number of possible sub-locations may vary depending on the specific location indicated by the second set of bits in different entries. In other words, different locations within the first-pool memories may contain data organized into varying numbers of sub-locations, yet the bit-width dedicated to representing sub-location addressing remains constant.

This fixed-width design offers several practical advantages:

- **Simplified Entry Format**: By maintaining a consistent bit-width for the third set of bits, all second-set entries share a uniform overall structure, simplifying the design of hardware or software mechanisms that parse and interpret these entries.

- **Predictable Addressing Logic**: Fixed-width sub-location fields allow addressing logic to be implemented generically, without requiring entry-specific or location-specific variations in bit-field parsing.

- **Flexible Data Organization**: Despite the fixed bit-width, the method accommodates variable numbers of sub-locations across different memory locations, allowing the underlying data organization to remain flexible while the addressing mechanism remains standardized.

- **Efficient Use of Reserved Bits**: In cases where a particular location has fewer sub-locations than the maximum representable by the fixed bit-width, the unused bit combinations may be reserved, ignored, or otherwise handled without disrupting the overall addressing scheme.

## Conclusion

This method thus provides a robust and flexible framework for organizing and accessing memory across two distinct pools. By combining page-level, location-level, and sub-location-level addressing within each second-set entry—while maintaining a fixed bit-width for the finest level of granularity—the method achieves an effective balance between addressing precision, structural consistency, and adaptability to varying data organizations within the first-pool memories.

# Method for Configuring Memory Pools with Cross-Referenced Entry Sets

## Overview

This disclosure describes a method and system for configuring memory pools to implement two interrelated sets of entries within a computing or networking system. The approach enables efficient storage and cross-referencing between a first pool of memory entries and a second pool that references the first, using a structured addressing scheme that balances flexibility with implementation efficiency.

## Detailed Description

### First Memory Pool Configuration

The first pool of memories is configured to store a first set of entries at specific, identifiable locations. Each entry in this first set occupies a designated location within the memory pool, and these locations serve as the target destinations that will be referenced by entries in the second pool. The organization of the first pool may be structured such that different locations can accommodate varying amounts of data or varying numbers of sub-elements, depending on the specific requirements of the entries being stored.

### Second Memory Pool Configuration

The second pool of memories is configured to implement a second set of entries, where each entry in this second set is structured to contain three distinct categories of bits:

1. **Page-indicating bits**: These bits identify or specify which page within the memory architecture is being referenced, allowing the system to navigate to the correct memory page before further address resolution occurs.

2. **Location-specifying bits**: These bits identify the specific location within the identified page where the referenced first-set entry resides. This provides the coarse-grained addressing needed to locate the target entry.

3. **Sub-location-specifying bits**: These bits provide fine-grained addressing within the specified location, allowing the second-set entry to reference a particular sub-location within that location.

Together, these three categories of bits enable each second-set entry to construct a complete reference or pointer to a specific first-set entry stored in the first memory pool.

### Key Architectural Feature: Fixed Bit Allocation with Variable Sub-Location Count

The significant and distinguishing aspect of this configuration method lies in the relationship between the sub-location-specifying bits and the actual sub-locations they reference:

- **Fixed bit width**: The number of bits allocated for the sub-location-specifying field remains constant and uniform across all entries in the second set. This means that every second-set entry, regardless of what it references, uses the same fixed number of bits for this portion of its addressing scheme.

- **Variable sub-location count**: Despite this fixed bit allocation, the actual number of sub-locations that exist within different locations (as referenced by different second-set entries) can vary. In other words, one location within the first pool might contain a different number of addressable sub-locations than another location, even though the second-set entries referencing them use the same number of bits to specify a sub-location.

### Advantages of This Approach

This design provides several benefits for system implementation:

- **Uniform entry structure**: By maintaining a fixed bit-width for the sub-location field across all second-set entries, the hardware or software implementing this scheme can use consistent, simplified logic for parsing and processing second-set entries, regardless of which first-set location they ultimately reference.

- **Flexible resource allocation**: Because the actual number of sub-locations can vary by location, the underlying memory architecture retains flexibility to allocate resources non-uniformly across different locations in the first pool, optimizing for the specific needs of different entries or use cases without requiring changes to the second-set entry format.

- **Efficient cross-referencing**: This combination of fixed-width addressing fields with variable underlying resource allocation enables efficient and scalable cross-referencing between the two memory pools, as the system can accommodate heterogeneous data structures in the first pool while maintaining a homogeneous, easily-decodable addressing scheme in the second pool.

- **Simplified decoding logic**: Since all second-set entries share the same bit-width allocation scheme (even though the practical use or range of the sub-location bits may differ based on the target location), the decoding and addressing logic required to interpret these entries can be implemented uniformly, reducing complexity in the overall system design.

This method thus achieves an effective balance between structural uniformity (which simplifies implementation and control logic) and functional flexibility (which allows the underlying memory organization to adapt to varying data requirements across different locations), making it particularly well-suited for applications requiring efficient memory management with variable-sized or variably-structured data groupings.

# ABSTRACT

A method and system for configuring memory pools in a computing environment is disclosed, wherein a first set of memory pool entries is structured to reference a second set of memory pool entries through a hierarchical addressing scheme comprising pages, locations, and sub-locations. Each memory pool entry includes an identifier composed of a fixed bit allocation and a variable bit allocation, wherein the fixed bit allocation designates a page within the memory pool and the variable bit allocation designates a location and a sub-location within the designated page. The method includes allocating a plurality of pages within a memory pool, each page comprising a plurality of locations, and each location comprising a plurality of sub-locations, such that entries within the first memory pool set reference corresponding entries within the second memory pool set via the page, location, and sub-location identifiers. The variable bit allocation is configurable based on a size of the memory pool, a number of pages, a number of locations per page, or a number of sub-locations per location, thereby enabling dynamic adjustment of addressing granularity without altering an overall bit-width of the entry identifier. The method further includes generating, updating, and traversing reference entries between the first and second memory pool sets based on the page, location, and sub-location identifiers, and resolving the referenced entry by decoding the fixed and variable bit allocations to access memory pool data associated with the sub-location. The disclosed configuration enables efficient memory pool cross-referencing, scalable addressing across memory pools of varying sizes, and reduced overhead in tracking inter-pool relationships, while supporting flexible reconfiguration of address bit-widths to accommodate different memory pool architectures and capacities.

# TECHNICAL DISCLOSURE

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to memory architectures for digital systems, and more particularly to a hierarchical memory organization employing two interconnected pools of unit memories wherein entries in a second memory pool reference storage locations within a first memory pool through structured addressing fields.

## BACKGROUND

Modern digital systems, including network processing devices, packet switching systems, and general-purpose computing architectures, often require efficient mechanisms for managing large numbers of discrete data structures with variable relationships between them. Conventional memory architectures typically employ flat addressing schemes or simple indexed lookup tables, which can become inefficient when data structures require multi-level referencing, shared storage of common elements, or dynamic allocation across variable-sized data structures.

In particular, applications involving linked-list structures, table-based lookups, forwarding information bases, and similar data organizations benefit from memory architectures that support indirection between pools of storage, particularly where one pool serves as a set of reusable "unit" storage elements referenced by entries in another pool. Existing solutions often require complex pointer arithmetic, external translation tables, or software-managed indirection layers, each of which introduces additional latency, complexity, and area/power overhead in hardware implementations.

There exists a need for a memory architecture that provides efficient, hardware-native indirection between two pools of unit memories using structured, decomposable addressing fields, thereby reducing lookup latency and simplifying address decode logic while enabling flexible allocation and referencing schemes.

## SUMMARY

In accordance with various embodiments, a memory architecture is disclosed comprising a first pool of unit memories and a second pool of unit memories, wherein each entry of the second pool of unit memories comprises an index value that is decomposed into a plurality of bit fields, including at least a page field, a location field, and a sub-location field, which together identify a specific unit memory entry, or portion thereof, within the first pool of unit memories.

This structured addressing enables the second pool to function as an indirection or reference layer over the first pool, wherein individual unit memories in the first pool may be organized into pages, wherein each page comprises a plurality of locations, and wherein each location may further comprise a plurality of sub-locations. The described architecture accordingly supports variable granularity of addressing and permits efficient sharing, reuse, and dynamic management of underlying storage elements in the first pool.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### Overview of the Architecture

Referring to the drawings, in one embodiment, the memory architecture comprises a first pool of unit memories 100 and a second pool of unit memories 200, both of which may be implemented using any suitable memory technology, including but not limited to SRAM, DRAM, register file arrays, content-addressable memory (CAM), or combinations thereof, arranged as physical or logical arrays of fixed-width storage units referred to herein as "unit memories."

The first pool of unit memories 100 is organized as a plurality of individually addressable storage units, each capable of storing a data value, pointer, payload, or other data structure as required by the particular application. The first pool 100 is logically subdivided into a hierarchy of addressable subdivisions, including:

- **Pages**: The first pool 100 is divided into a plurality of pages, each page comprising a contiguous or non-contiguous set of unit memory locations.
- **Locations**: Each page is further subdivided into a plurality of locations, each location representing an individually addressable unit memory or a group of related unit memories within a given page.
- **Sub-locations**: Each location may optionally be subdivided into a plurality of sub-locations, wherein each sub-location represents a smaller addressable portion of a unit memory location, such as a byte lane, sub-word, or bit-field segment.

The second pool of unit memories 200 comprises a plurality of entries 210, each entry comprising an index value 220 used to reference a corresponding storage location in the first pool 100. In accordance with the disclosed architecture, the index value 220 is not treated as a monolithic address but is instead decomposed into a plurality of discrete bit fields, including:

1. **Page Field (222)**: A first bit field of the index value 220 that identifies a specific page within the first pool of unit memories 100.
2. **Location Field (224)**: A second bit field of the index value 220 that identifies a specific location within the page identified by the page field 222.
3. **Sub-Location Field (226)**: A third bit field of the index value 220 that identifies a specific sub-location within the location identified by the location field 224.

### Structural Diagram Description

**FIG. 1** illustrates a block diagram of the overall memory architecture, showing the second pool of unit memories 200 coupled to the first pool of unit memories 100 through an address decode/translation logic block 300. The address decode/translation logic 300 receives the index value 220 from a given entry 210 of the second pool 200 and parses the index value 220 into its constituent bit fields—page field 222, location field 224, and sub-location field 226—in order to generate a physical or logical address into the first pool of unit memories 100.

**FIG. 2** illustrates the bit-field decomposition of an exemplary index value 220, showing the relative bit positions and widths of the page field 222, location field 224, and sub-location field 226. In one embodiment, the page field 222 occupies the most-significant bits of the index value 220, the location field 224 occupies an intermediate group of bits, and the sub-location field 226 occupies the least-significant bits, though it will be appreciated that other orderings and bit-widths may be employed without departing from the scope of this disclosure.

**FIG. 3** illustrates the hierarchical organization of the first pool of unit memories 100, showing a plurality of pages 110(1)–110(N), each page comprising a plurality of locations 120(1)–120(M), and each location further comprising a plurality of sub-locations 130(1)–130(K).

### Addressing and Lookup Operation

In operation, a requesting entity (e.g., a processing element, packet classification engine, control-plane process, or hardware state machine) accesses an entry 210 in the second pool of unit memories 200 based on a given lookup key, hash value, or sequential index. The index value 220 stored in the accessed entry 210 is provided to the address decode/translation logic 300.

The address decode/translation logic 300 extracts the page field 222 to select the target page 110(*n*) within the first pool 100. The location field 224 is then used to select a specific location 120(*m*) within the selected page 110(*n*). Finally, if applicable, the sub-location field 226 is used to select a specific sub-location 130(*k*) within the selected location 120(*m*), thereby resolving the complete reference down to the desired granularity of storage.

In embodiments where the underlying data structure stored at a given location does not require sub-location addressing, the sub-location field 226 may be omitted, set to a default value, or reserved for future use, and the address decode/translation logic 300 may treat the location field 224 as fully resolving the address within the first pool 100.

### Variable Bit-Field Widths and Configurability

In certain embodiments, the respective widths of the page field 222, location field 224, and sub-location field 226 are configurable, either at design time via synthesis parameters or at run time via configuration registers, to accommodate different sizes of the first pool of unit memories 100 and different granularities of addressing. For example, a system requiring a larger number of pages but fewer locations per page may configure the index value 220 with a wider page field 222 and a narrower location field 224, whereas a system requiring finer sub-location granularity may allocate additional bits to the sub-location field 226 at the expense of the location field 224 or page field 222.

This configurability may be implemented using configurable field-width registers within the address decode/translation logic 300, wherein the boundaries between the page field 222, location field 224, and sub-location field 226 are defined by one or more configuration parameters, such as a page-field-width register, a location-field-width register, or equivalent structures. This allows a single hardware implementation to be adapted to varying capacities of the first pool of unit memories 100 without requiring redesign of the second pool of unit memories 200 or the address decode/translation logic 300.

### Allocation and Management of the First Pool

In various embodiments, the first pool of unit memories 100 is managed by an allocation unit (not explicitly shown, but understood to be present in various embodiments) that tracks the availability of pages, locations, and sub-locations within the first pool 100, for example via a free-list, bitmap, or similar data structure. When a new data structure is to be stored, the allocation unit selects an available page, location, and, if applicable, sub-location within the first pool 100, and returns the corresponding page field 222, location field 224, and sub-location field 226 values, which are then assembled into an index value 220 and written into a corresponding entry 210 of the second pool of unit memories 200.

This allocation scheme advantageously allows multiple entries 210 in the second pool 200 to reference the same, or overlapping, regions of the first pool 100, thereby enabling data sharing, reference counting, or copy-on-write semantics, depending on the requirements of the particular application. Additionally, the hierarchical page/location/sub-location organization of the first pool 100 permits localized allocation and deallocation operations (e.g., freeing all locations within a given page) without requiring individual tracking of every unit memory within the pool.

### Example Application: Linked Data Structures

In one exemplary, non-limiting application, the disclosed architecture may be employed to implement a linked-list or tree-based data structure, wherein each entry 210 of the second pool 200 represents a node of the list or tree, and the index value 220 stored therein identifies the location, within the first pool 100, of the node's associated payload data or of a subsequent linked node. By decomposing the index value 220 into page field 222, location field 224, and sub-location field 226, the architecture permits efficient traversal of the underlying data structure using simple field-extraction logic, without requiring a full address translation table or content-addressable lookup.

### Example Application: Packet Forwarding / Table Lookup

In another exemplary, non-limiting application, the first pool of unit memories 100 may store forwarding table entries, classification rules, or similar network-processing data structures, organized into pages corresponding to different table partitions, locations corresponding to individual table rows, and sub-locations corresponding to individual fields within a table row (e.g., destination address, priority, action code). The second pool of unit memories 200 may then store index values 220 resulting from a hash lookup, longest-prefix match, or other classification operation, wherein the resulting index value 220 is decomposed by the address decode/translation logic 300 to directly address the relevant page, location, and sub-location within the first pool 100, thereby retrieving the required forwarding or classification data with minimal latency.

## ALTERNATIVE EMBODIMENTS

It will be appreciated by those skilled in the art that:

- The number of hierarchical bit fields need not be limited to three (page, location, sub-location), and additional or fewer bit fields may be employed, including additional levels of indirection (e.g., a "bank" field or "super-page" field) without departing from the scope of this disclosure.
- The first pool of unit memories 100 and second pool of unit memories 200 may be implemented in the same physical memory array, in separate physical memory arrays, or in a distributed fashion across multiple memory banks or memory technologies.
- The address decode/translation logic 300 may be implemented as combinational logic, a lookup table, a small programmable state machine, or any combination thereof.
- Entries 210 in the second pool 200 may include additional metadata alongside the index value 220, such as validity bits, reference counts, type tags, or protection attributes, which may be used in conjunction with the page field 222, location field 224, and sub-location field 226 to control access to the first pool of unit memories 100.
- The bit ordering of the page field 222, location field 224, and sub-location field 226 within the index value 220 may be rearranged, interleaved, or encoded (e.g., via Gray coding or other encoding schemes) without departing from the underlying inventive concept of hierarchical, field-based indirection between the second pool 200 and the first pool 100.

# Patent Claim Summary: Cross-Referenced Memory Management System

## Field of Invention

This disclosure relates to hardware memory management systems, and more particularly to systems and methods for managing memory allocation using cross-referenced entry sets stored across distinct memory pools, wherein individual entries support variable numbers of associated sub-locations.

---

## Claim 1 (Independent — System Claim)

A hardware memory management system comprising:

a first memory pool configured to store a first set of entries, each entry in the first set comprising:
  (i) an identifier field;
  (ii) a cross-reference field configured to reference one or more corresponding entries in a second set of entries; and
  (iii) a sub-location count field indicating a variable number of sub-locations associated with said entry;

a second memory pool, physically or logically distinct from the first memory pool, configured to store the second set of entries, each entry in the second set comprising a reverse cross-reference field configured to reference one or more corresponding entries in the first set of entries;

a memory controller communicatively coupled to the first memory pool and the second memory pool, configured to:
  (a) resolve a memory access request by traversing the cross-reference field of a first-set entry to locate a corresponding second-set entry;
  (b) allocate or deallocate sub-locations within an entry based on the variable sub-location count field, independent of sub-location counts associated with other entries in the first set; and
  (c) maintain referential consistency between the first set and the second set upon modification, addition, or removal of an entry in either set.

---

## Claim 2 (Dependent)

The system of claim 1, wherein the sub-location count field for a given entry in the first set is dynamically adjustable during runtime without requiring reallocation of sub-location counts for other entries in the first set.

## Claim 3 (Dependent)

The system of claim 1, wherein the memory controller is further configured to detect and resolve a broken or dangling cross-reference resulting from deletion of an entry, by updating the corresponding reverse cross-reference field in the second memory pool.

## Claim 4 (Dependent)

The system of claim 1, wherein the first memory pool and the second memory pool operate at different clock domains, and wherein the memory controller comprises synchronization logic to coordinate cross-referenced access between the domains.

## Claim 5 (Dependent)

The system of claim 1, wherein each sub-location within an entry of the first set is individually addressable and comprises a status flag indicating one of: allocated, free, or reserved.

## Claim 6 (Dependent)

The system of claim 1, wherein the cross-reference field comprises a pointer, index, or hash value uniquely identifying a corresponding entry in the second set.

## Claim 7 (Dependent)

The system of claim 1, further comprising a validation circuit configured to verify bidirectional consistency between the cross-reference field of a first-set entry and the reverse cross-reference field of its corresponding second-set entry during a read or write operation.

---

## Claim 8 (Independent — Method Claim)

A method for managing hardware memory comprising:

storing a first set of entries in a first memory pool, each entry having a variable sub-location count;

storing a second set of entries in a second memory pool distinct from the first memory pool;

establishing cross-references between entries of the first set and corresponding entries of the second set;

receiving a memory access request;

resolving the memory access request by traversing a cross-reference from an entry in the first set to a corresponding entry in the second set;

dynamically allocating or deallocating sub-locations within an entry of the first set based on the variable sub-location count associated with that entry; and

maintaining referential integrity between the first set and the second set in response to a change affecting either set.

---

## Claim 9 (Dependent)

The method of claim 8, further comprising adjusting the sub-location count of a first entry in the first set without affecting the sub-location count of a second, different entry in the first set.

## Claim 10 (Dependent)

The method of claim 8, further comprising detecting a modification to an entry in the second set and propagating a corresponding update to the cross-reference field of an associated entry in the first set.

---

## Notes for Prosecution Counsel

# METHOD FOR HIERARCHICAL MEMORY POOL ORGANIZATION WITH ENCODED REFERENCE ENTRIES

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to memory management systems, and more particularly to methods and systems for organizing memory resources into a plurality of pools, wherein entries in one pool encode multi-level addressing information to reference data stored in another pool.

## BACKGROUND

In various computing environments, memory resources may be organized to optimize access patterns, reduce redundancy, and improve overall system efficiency. Conventional memory addressing schemes may suffer from inefficiencies when large datasets must be referenced repeatedly across disparate locations, resulting in increased memory overhead and reduced performance. Accordingly, there exists a need in the art for improved methods of organizing memory into functionally distinct pools, wherein compact encoded references may be utilized to locate and retrieve underlying data with reduced storage overhead.

## SUMMARY

In accordance with one embodiment, a method is provided for organizing a memory into at least a first pool and a second pool. According to some embodiments, the first pool may be configured to store a plurality of data elements, which may include, without limitation, data blocks, data segments, records, values, or any other suitable unit of information as may be appreciated by one of ordinary skill in the art. In certain embodiments, the second pool may be configured to store a plurality of entries, wherein each such entry comprises an encoded reference to one or more data elements stored within the first pool.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### General Architecture

Referring now to the drawings, in which like reference numerals refer to like elements throughout the several views, there is shown in accordance with one or more embodiments a method for organizing memory into a first pool and a second pool. It will be appreciated that although the present description proceeds with reference to specific exemplary embodiments, the disclosed methods and systems are not so limited, and may be implemented in any of a number of alternative configurations without departing from the spirit and scope of the present disclosure.

In one embodiment, the method comprises allocating a first region of memory as a first pool and allocating a second region of memory as a second pool. It should be understood that the first pool and the second pool may be physically distinct regions of memory, logically distinct regions of a shared physical memory, or any combination thereof, and further that the pools may reside on a single memory device or may be distributed across a plurality of memory devices communicatively coupled to one another, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.

### Structure of Second-Pool Entries

According to certain embodiments, each entry of the plurality of entries stored in the second pool comprises, at minimum, three constituent components, referred to herein for convenience as page bits, location bits, and sub-location bits, although it will be understood that additional or alternative components may be included in various embodiments without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.

In some embodiments, the page bits comprise a first plurality of bits configured to identify, at least in part, a page of the first pool within which a corresponding data element is stored. It will be appreciated that, as used herein, the term "page" refers generally to a defined subdivision of the first pool, and may correspond to a fixed-size block of memory, a variable-size block of memory, or any other logical or physical subdivision as may be appropriate to a given implementation. In certain embodiments, the first pool may be subdivided into a plurality of pages, each such page being uniquely identifiable by a corresponding value of the page bits.

In some embodiments, the location bits comprise a second plurality of bits configured to identify, at least in part, a location within the identified page at which the corresponding data element, or a portion thereof, is stored. It will be understood that, in various embodiments, the location bits may specify an offset, an index, a row, a column, or any other suitable locational parameter within the identified page, and that the particular scheme employed may vary depending upon the underlying architecture of the first pool without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.

In some embodiments, the sub-location bits comprise a third plurality of bits configured to identify, at least in part, a sub-location within the identified location at which the corresponding data element, or a portion thereof, is stored. In certain embodiments, the sub-location bits may further refine the addressing granularity provided by the location bits, such that a combination of the page bits, the location bits, and the sub-location bits collectively and uniquely identifies a specific data element, or portion thereof, within the first pool. It will be appreciated that the sub-location bits may, in some embodiments, identify a byte offset, a bit offset, a sub-block, a sub-record, or any other suitable subdivision of the identified location, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.

### Encoding and Combination of Bit Fields

In accordance with various embodiments, the page bits, the location bits, and the sub-location bits may be concatenated, interleaved, or otherwise combined according to a predetermined encoding scheme so as to form a composite reference value stored within the corresponding entry of the second pool. In some embodiments, the composite reference value may be of a fixed bit-length, such that each entry within the second pool occupies a substantially uniform amount of storage, thereby facilitating efficient indexing and retrieval operations. In alternative embodiments, the composite reference value may be of variable bit-length, depending upon, for example, the size of the first pool, the number of pages therein, or other implementation-specific considerations.

It will be further appreciated that, in some embodiments, the relative bit-widths allocated to the page bits, the location bits, and the sub-location bits, respectively, may be configured based upon a desired addressing capacity at each respective level of the hierarchy. For example, in one non-limiting embodiment, a greater number of bits may be allocated to the page bits in implementations wherein the first pool comprises a relatively large number of pages, whereas a lesser number of bits may be allocated to the sub-location bits in implementations wherein a relatively coarse addressing granularity is sufficient. It should be understood that any suitable bit-width allocation may be employed, and that the specific values disclosed herein are provided by way of example only and not by way of limitation.

### Method of Operation

In operation, according to one embodiment, the method further comprises receiving a request to access a data element, the request specifying, directly or indirectly, an entry within the second pool. Responsive to receiving the request, the method may further comprise retrieving the specified entry from the second pool, and decoding the entry so as to extract therefrom the page bits, the location bits, and the sub-location bits. The method may further comprise determining, based upon the extracted page bits, a corresponding page of the first pool; determining, based upon the extracted location bits, a corresponding location within the determined page; and determining, based upon the extracted sub-location bits, a corresponding sub-location within the determined location. The method may further comprise retrieving the data element, or the requested portion thereof, from the first pool based upon the determined page, the determined location, and the determined sub-location.

It will be appreciated that, in some embodiments, the foregoing decoding and retrieval operations may be performed by a memory controller, a processor, a dedicated hardware logic circuit, firmware, software executing on a general-purpose processor, or any combination thereof, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.

### Advantages and Alternative Embodiments

It will be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art that the hierarchical encoding scheme disclosed herein may, in certain embodiments, provide various advantages, including without limitation reduced storage overhead for reference entries, improved efficiency in locating and retrieving data elements within the first pool, and enhanced scalability with respect to increasing sizes of the first pool. However, it should be understood that the foregoing advantages are provided by way of example only, and that not all embodiments necessarily achieve any or all of the stated advantages.

While the foregoing has described a first pool and a second pool, it will be appreciated that, in alternative embodiments, additional pools may be provided, and that entries within any given pool may reference data elements or entries within one or more other pools according to analogous encoding schemes, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure. Furthermore, although the page bits, location bits, and sub-location bits have been described herein as a three-level hierarchy, it will be understood that additional levels of hierarchy may be incorporated in certain embodiments, and that the specific number of hierarchical levels disclosed herein is provided by way of example only and not by way of limitation.

### Exemplary System Implementation

In accordance with a further embodiment, there is provided a system comprising a memory and a processor operatively coupled to the memory, wherein the memory is organized into a first pool and a second pool substantially as described hereinabove, and wherein the processor is configured to execute instructions for performing the method steps disclosed herein. It will be appreciated that the system may further comprise additional components, including without limitation one or more communication interfaces, one or more input/output devices, and one or more additional processors, without departing from the scope of the present disclosure.

## CONCLUSION

It is to be understood that the embodiments described herein are illustrative of the principles of the present disclosure and that various modifications may be made by those skilled in the art without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Accordingly, it is intended that the scope of the invention be limited only by the appended claims and their equivalents.
